meta.scope: Core system rules, the Warp Shell player/loot content, and the universal monster/loot frameworks, extracted for the Warp Shell campaign tool's generation, encounter-building, and stat block export logic. Flavor/lore text has been paraphrased into short descriptors; mechanical text (dice, numbers, item one-liners) is kept close to source since it is functional game data rather than narrative prose.
meta.note: Page numbers below are approximate, from the book's own printed page numbers (not PDF page index).

effort.description: Roll EFFORT after a successful ATTEMPT to resolve how much damage/progress it produces. Also used to gauge how much is needed to overcome a task or foe.

basic.use: Bare hands or wits — punches, brute-force breaks, deciphering, etc.

weaponsAndTools.use: Standard melee/ranged weapons, or tools used to accomplish a task (pry bar, bandages, torch).

magicAndEnergy.use: Explosive magic, arcane/energy effects (particle beams, lasers, plasma), and magical healing.

ultimate.use: In play: added ON TOP of the base EFFORT die on a natural 20 ATTEMPT roll (critical success). It is ALSO one of the trainable categories at character creation (Step 3: Boost Effort Types) — the 4 EFFORT bonus points can give a character affinity for weapons, magic, or "the risky business of ULTIMATE," same as the other 4 categories.

descriptions.WIS: Intuition, perception, nature sense, danger sense.
descriptions.CHA: Persuasion, force of will, resisting fear, intimidation.

characterCreation.arrayNote: Freely distributed across the 6 STATS at character creation (e.g. all 6 in one STAT, or 1 in each).
characterCreation.maxStatBonusNote: No STAT can ever exceed +10, regardless of source (base points, LIFE FORM, LOOT).

inventory.rule: Inventory is limited to 10 CARRIED items and 10 EQUIPPED items — two separate pools, not one shared total.
inventory.carriedVsEquipped: CARRIED items must be EQUIPPED to offer any benefit or be used — something sitting in your pack (not actively worn/wielded) is inert until you swap it into an EQUIPPED slot, which may mean swapping something else out.
inventory.note: Individual LOOT items can state their own slot cost (e.g. Adamantium Armor occupies 5 slots, a Blaster occupies none) — that cost applies to whichever pool (CARRIED or EQUIPPED) the item is currently placed in.

defense.formula: DEFENSE = your CON STAT bonus + all DEFENSE bonuses granted by LOOT (armor, shields, etc.)
defense.maxDefenseNote: No character can exceed +10 DEFENSE no matter the total of CON and LOOT bonuses.
defense.playerDefenseRoll: When the GM calls for a DEFENSE roll (a danger/enemy ability affecting you), roll d20 + DEFENSE and meet or beat the current TARGET.
defense.enemyAttackTarget: When an enemy makes an ATTEMPT against a player, it does NOT roll against the scene TARGET — it rolls its STR or DEX bonus vs. 10 + the player's DEFENSE instead.

whenToCallForDefense: Shrapnel: any effect that sprays damage everywhere/in all directions — DEFENSE reduces or avoids it.
Falling: DEFENSE doesn't nullify fall damage, just reduces it.
All or Nothing: if an effect would drop a character to 0 HP or cause instant death, a final DEFENSE roll may decide if they're merely knocked out vs. destroyed.
Immovable: resisting being shoved/slid/toppled by sheer force rewards heavily-armored characters.
Shared Defenses: characters fighting shoulder-to-shoulder can add/share DEFENSE bonuses or allow re-rolls on failure.

No Defense (auto-hit): bigger/badder attacks (e.g. a dragon's tail swipe) don't roll to attack at all — they simply hit, and the target absorbs the impact as best they can. Useful for keeping boss fights fast.
damagingDefenses: Sunder attacks: monster abilities specifically built to strip armor LOOT (e.g. "you take 12 damage and lose 1D4 DEFENSE").
Corrosion: acid, rust, extreme temperature crack/dissolve equipment, lowering DEFENSE.
Massive damage: a hit over 20 damage plausibly damages armor too.
Overclocker: a shield used constantly loses 1 DEFENSE per session from wear.
The Yanking: grabby/tentacled/thieving enemies steal armor pieces on a successful attack.

target.description: A single number in play for the current scene. All CHECK/ATTEMPT rolls (d20 + a relevant STAT) must meet or beat it to succeed.

conditions: Character already tried and failed the same action last TURN
Character is being helped by another character
Obstacle is rickety or barely intact
The task is very simple or obvious
Character is far larger than the obstacle
Character has time to be careful
Character has had repeated successes with similar tasks
Character has special LOOT or a temporary effect that helps
Success would be superhuman or extraordinary
Character is badly injured or stunned
Character is in a big hurry
Extreme environmental conditions (cold, heat, rain, wind)

escalation.rule: The GM raises the TARGET when a scene should feel more dangerous (new encounter phase, weather turning, a big enemy effect), typically stepping it up (or down, as hazards ease) by small increments such as 1 per ROUND in a dynamic hazard.
escalation.note: This escalation applies to the scene TARGET used for player rolls. Enemy attacks against players always target 10 + player DEFENSE instead (see defense.enemyAttackTarget).

chosenTargets.description: "All encounters start with a TARGET of 10, 12, 15, or 18" — a GM shortcut that narrows the "what should the TARGET be" question down to 4 values instead of picking anywhere in 10-18.

values.10: Beginner encounters, easy conditions, home base, clear weather or high ground. Players will dominate.
values.12: The supreme average TARGET — used in almost all encounters. A level playing field that just always feels right.
values.15: For a group with experience or good gear, rough conditions, low light, smoke, cramped spaces, or frightening situations — enough challenge to demand creative thinking.
values.18: Brutal. Almost impossible for players; forces them to find a way to lower the number immediately. Reserve for the most difficult/confusing/obscured conditions, including magically-induced obstacles.

targetDamage.description: Players reducing the current TARGET through clever play, LOOT, or abilities (e.g. a torch reducing a dark-catacomb TARGET of 15 to 14). The environment/enemies can likewise increase or randomize the TARGET.
targetDamage.targetMinimum: As a rule, players can never reduce a TARGET by more than 3 points below where the GM set it (a 15 can never go below 12).

deathAndRecovery.zeroHP: At 0 HP a character falls unconscious. Any SPELLS/effects they were sustaining end immediately.
deathAndRecovery.dyingRoll: On the character's NEXT TURN after reaching 0 HP, roll 1d4. That is how many ROUNDS remain before death, absent aid or a MIRACLE.
deathAndRecovery.miracle: On each TURN while DYING, the character may roll a d20. A natural 20 revives them at 1 HP.
deathAndRecovery.deathFinal: If all DYING ROUNDS pass with no help and no MIRACLE rolled, the character dies — no further rolls or saves.
deathAndRecovery.blownToBits: Taking damage down to -20 HP in a single instant destroys the character outright: no body, no recovery.

recoverAction.description: Spend a TURN to catch your breath and bind wounds.
recoverAction.roll: d20 + CON STAT vs. current TARGET

stabilizeAlly.description: "Don't Die On Me, Man!" — an ally who can reach the DYING character attempts to stabilize them.
stabilizeAlly.roll: INT or WIS STAT vs. current TARGET
stabilizeAlly.onSuccess: The DYING timer stops. The character remains unconscious but stable.

fields.hearts: 1 HEART = 10 HP. A suggestion only — tune to the table.
fields.rolls: STAT bonuses simplified to one or two values, covering CHECKS, ATTEMPTS, and EFFORT.
fields.actionsAndTraits: Combat actions or special/unique aspects of the creature.
fields.lore: A one-line summary of concept and motivation.

I.label: Tier I — Mooks/minions/wimps/chumps
I.notes: A "super mook" variant has only 1 HP and no STAT bonus at all.

II.label: Tier II — Standard enemy
II.notes: Give it one interesting piece of gear or a unique attack ability.

III.label: Tier III — Sub-boss / "wimp gate"
III.notes: Often has damage immunity. At least 1 special ability: area blast, HP drain, or insta-kill without a roll.

IV.label: Tier IV — Apex / world-ending
IV.notes: Damage immunity plus a self-healing action. At least 1 special ability: area blast, escape-and-heal, summon reinforcements, destroy gear, or alter environment/target/timer. Even when "defeated," it is rarely gone for good.

designToolkit.description: Suggested special-ability hooks for hand-built monsters, beyond raw STAT/HEART totals.
options: Repel them (shove away, dangerous combined with ranged barrage)
Negate their attacks (cost them a turn)
Bolster defenses (double HEARTS or make attacks HARD for a turn)
Paralyze (with a CON check to break free)
Lots of actions (2-3+ for boss quality)
Go enraged at a threshold (ULTIMATE or higher STATS)
An unlikely foe (animate an object/place as the monster)

monsters.warpShellNote: The core book's alphabetical Monster Listings (Agnar, Angel, Avenger, Ant Men, Demon, Ogre, etc.) are fantasy-flavored, not sci-fi. There is no literal "Mutant Reptoid" stat block in the source. For Warp Shell antagonists (Reptoid commandos, Xevosian troops, Xill constructs, rogue MECHA), build from the Tier framework above and flavor with warpShellLifeForms traits below — that combination is the intended Warp Shell monster-building method.

lootEconomy.description: Reference pricing in COIN, useful for the purchase method of progression and for sanity-checking generated loot against a rarity/value tier.
lootEconomy.coinValue: 1 COIN is fair pay for 1 day's work.

pricing.item: Meal and bed for a night

warpShellLifeForms.description: The playable species ("LIFE FORMS") of Warp Shell. Each grants a stat/mechanical bonus plus a choice of background flavor.

gmToolkit.sourceNote: GM's Guide material extracted separately from the character-creation/monster/loot content above — covers rewards, pacing, and encounter/vehicle design tools.

heroCoin.description: Awarded when a player does something that makes the game more fun for everyone. A shiny token that can be redeemed by that player OR handed to a worthy ally to redeem instead, at any time.
heroCoin.redeemEffect: Re-roll any roll, OR add ULTIMATE EFFORT on an EFFORT roll.
heroCoin.limit: A player can only hold 1 HERO COIN at a time.

milestoneReward.description: Each hero type has its own pool of LOOT-based upgrades (see warpShellRoles[type].milestoneAbilities). Awarded when a player turns a corner, discovers their destiny, or completes a lifelong quest — the GM can assign one directly or let the player choose from their pool, whichever fits the moment.
milestoneReward.cadence: A player should be earning one of these roughly every other session — not a hard rule, a pacing guideline.

movementAndDistance.description: ICRPG uses 4 loose bands instead of measured distance: CLOSE, NEAR, FAR, or OUT OF RANGE. Not exact measurement — it's about what's thematically within reach.

bands.close: Fingertip reach, standing still. No move needed to use or interact with CLOSE things.
bands.near: A few hurried steps. How far you can move in a TURN and still have time left for an ACTION.
bands.far: Several seconds to run — a bowshot, a thrown baseball, a hard pistol shot. Moving FAR on your TURN takes the ENTIRE turn (normally no action left after).
bands.outOfRange: Beyond FAR — can't be reached in one TURN of movement, and no effect can reach it. Allies OUT OF RANGE of each other can't help one another.

turnOrder.default: ICRPG's default is CLOCKWISE TURNS, board-game style, not a rolled initiative — the GM takes a turn to run monsters/hazards, players take turns in seating order around the table. No roll is required by default.
turnOrder.optionalInitiativeRoll: If a table prefers rolled initiative, roll a D20, unmodified, to see who starts the sequence when the action kicks in. Worth using deliberately: if the GM wins that roll, things escalate fast.
turnOrder.seatingStrategy: Players can use seating order tactically — e.g. seating the party's healer to the GM's right guarantees a heal lands right before the GM's turn; seating a tank first puts them in front of the action.
turnOrder.surpriseNote: The GM narrating who acts first based on the fiction (an ambush, a guard rounding a corner) is a normal, RAW-consistent GM call under the default clockwise system — it isn't a substitute for a formal roll-off unless the table has opted into rolled initiative.

sessionEndRoll.description: When something big happens (a supreme villain falls, a character dies, or the group is visibly tired), roll it out: roll 1d4, re-roll a 1. That many ROUNDS from now, the session ends — win or lose, wherever the action lands.
sessionEndRoll.finalFrame: Go around the table one last time and have each player describe how their character ends the episode, like the final frame of a comic panel.
sessionEndRoll.cliffhanger: The most exciting version: call for the session-end roll right at the climax of a battle, ending the night mid-peril.

sessionPacing.planOneSessionAtATime: Put full prep energy into a single night of play rather than a sprawling campaign outline — the session is the unit of GM planning in ICRPG.

dew.description: Every encounter needs Danger (real consequences if the group fails, not just damage/death), Energy (keep the table's pace brisk — call character names, not player names, cut anything that causes a lull), and Wonder (make one element of the scene huge, ancient, or awe-inspiring instead of a generic threat).

threeTs.description: Every room/encounter should include a Timer (a ticking d4 "suspense die," counted down each GM turn, that triggers something when it hits 0), a Threat (the monster/trap/hazard itself), and a Treat (at least one discoverable advantage — a lever, a weak point, stashed gear — that rewards players who investigate instead of brute-forcing it).

threeDs.description: Dials for tuning encounter difficulty: Damage (upgrade a weapon's die, e.g. d6 to 2d6, or scale an enemy's damage dice to its HEART count), Disruption (the environment itself as a weapon — mild/normal/extreme tiers of hazards like wind, falling debris, or reality-breaking cataclysms), and Duration (constrain how long the fight can last with a TIMER — the tighter the clock, the harder the fight).

roomArchetypes.note: TARGET values are loose suggestions based on complexity, meant to be adjusted, not fixed.

archetypes.name: Barrier
archetypes.description: A wall/chasm/barricade stands between the party and the exit. Can be as simple as jumping a crack, or as involved as a combination-locked energy field with pursuers closing in.

archetypes.name: Tangle
archetypes.description: Grabby/grappling hazards sit at the corners of the room with a safe zone in the middle; doors are offset to increase the risk of getting caught.

archetypes.name: Lock
archetypes.description: Players must search off-path for a key or release mechanism to a locked door, rather than simply smashing through.

archetypes.name: Kite
archetypes.description: An enemy is flanked by healers that make brute-force damage useless — players must lure the healers out of their healing zone.

archetypes.name: Pinch
archetypes.description: A narrow space (canyon, rift) where a few players must hold off a large enemy force — a funneling chokepoint fight.

archetypes.name: Ambush
archetypes.description: A visible first enemy draws players in while a larger hidden force waits to pounce from behind cover.

archetypes.name: Siege
archetypes.description: Attackers face a dug-in, higher-ground fortification; direct assault is near-impossible, forcing diversions or trickery.

archetypes.name: Tightrope
archetypes.description: Crossing a narrow elevated walkway above a pit of monsters — failure means a fall into danger, not just a miss.

archetypes.name: Duel
archetypes.description: The prime enemy hides behind stalwart guardians/healers who can't be talked down, only physically cleared — then a final concealed threat is revealed. Kite and Ambush combined.

archetypes.name: Ally Kite
archetypes.description: A bare one-way room with straightforward enemies — best used as a change of pace, a story beat, or a rest between more complex encounters, not the centerpiece.

timers.description: A d4 "suspense die" placed in view and reduced by 1 each GM turn; when it hits 0, the telegraphed thing happens. Ticking it down early on a failed roll is a valid way to accelerate tension.

variants.worldTimer: A big, campaign/session-opening TIMER at its max value (e.g. a d12) for a large-scale ticking threat ("in 12 ROUNDS, the reactor overloads and vaporizes the planet").
variants.turnTimer: Counts TURNS instead of ROUNDS for a much faster, more brutal pace — even a 4 can resolve in under a full ROUND.
variants.staticDeathTimer: Replaces the DYING d4 roll with a flat 3 ROUNDS to stabilize a downed character — evens out the swinginess of the random DYING roll.
variants.reloadRecharge: A d4 reload/recharge TIMER on a specific weapon or spell to force gear/spell variety instead of one attack spammed every turn.
variants.effortSubstitute: For a long task after an initial success, just announce a flat TIMER ("D4 ROUNDS to decode the password") instead of tracking EFFORT point-by-point.
variants.timerDamage: Players can delay or hasten a TIMER with actions/LOOT, same idea as TARGET DAMAGE — e.g. fighting a fire delays a burn-timer by 1 ROUND per TURN spent, or pulling power cables on a charging mech delays its activation.

vehiclesAndChunks.description: Vehicles (up to full starships) are built from CHUNKS. Each CHUNK = 1 HEART of vehicle HP (5 HP for battle suits specifically), one key function or weapon, ~250 lbs of mass, and costs 1,000 coin. No vehicle exceeds 5 CHUNKS.
vehiclesAndChunks.combatRules: Vehicles inflict DOUBLE damage against those on foot. Pedestrians do HALF damage against vehicles. When a CHUNK hits 0 HP it's destroyed — that ability/weapon is lost, and it can become a battlefield hazard or scatter as wreckage.
vehiclesAndChunks.speedTiers: Slow and Fast engines use 1 CHUNK; Hyperfast engines use 2 CHUNKS.

examples.build: Cockpit (seats 2; pilots have 1D4 ROUNDS to live if destroyed while occupied), Ion Drive (deep-space travel; crippled to taxi/thruster speed if destroyed), SR Missile Pack (D10 CHUNK damage or destroys 1D8 microfighters, 8 bursts), Chain Gun (D8 CHUNK damage or destroys 1D4 microfighters, never reloads)

starfighterManeuvers: Punch It (move to an adjacent SECTOR)
Zero (lock onto and follow a target through a PUNCH IT)
Engage (fire guns; a hit rolls damage on a random CHUNK)
Break Off (stay put but elude pursuers this TURN)
Ditch (eject; roll to escape safely or take WEAPON DAMAGE)

horrorMode.description: Optional SANITY subsystem for horror-toned sessions. All sane characters start with 1 HEART of SANITY; it erodes from witnessing horrific/supernatural events and hits 0 at complete madness (non-functional).

sanityDamageTable.event: See a person dismembered, beheaded, or die terribly
Discover a corpse or scene of depravity
Stare directly at a supernatural entity/ghost/zombie
Lose a limb (or drop to 1 HP from a single hit)
Witness an object of celestial/trans-dimensional origin
Gaze upon an abomination from between worlds
Assemble clues leading to dark, cosmos-spanning truths
Witness the arrival of an Elder-God-scale entity
Form a mind-union with an Elder God or Beyonder

sanityStateOfBeing.10: Safe in the veil of daily normalcy
sanityStateOfBeing.8-9: Aghast/rationalizing, on edge, wary of unexplained sounds
sanityStateOfBeing.6-7: Shocked/terrified; CHA and WIS rolls HARD, cannot attack the source of fear
sanityStateOfBeing.4-5: All rolls HARD; must seek hiding or back away immediately
sanityStateOfBeing.2-3: Screaming/petrified 1D4 ROUNDS, or fleeing at max speed for 1D6 ROUNDS
sanityStateOfBeing.1: All rolls HARD is now permanent
sanityStateOfBeing.0: Catatonic, clinically mad, reliving the terror endlessly

adventureBuildingMethod.description: The Index Card method for building a full adventure in 4 steps.
steps: 1. The Whole Truth: write the bird's-eye secrets/twist/villain/scenery on one card — just the facts, no polish.

2. Scenes & Bullets: break it into 5 scenes (2-4 flavor bullets each) — typically: opening hook/guardian fight, a role-play dilemma, a big setback, the climactic battle, rewards + a twist that keeps the threat alive.
3. Casting Call: one index card per NPC/enemy needed for those scenes — if it doesn't fit on a card, it's too much detail for the table.
4. Make Some Maps: rough sketches (even sideways/blueprint-style) that reinforce mood and give players something to describe and act on, not precise grid measurement.
